note: Batch 1 broad survey of raw feature families across lookbacks to map which effects exist in this panel and their signs
Batch 2 refine the long horizon reversal family: horizons, log vs simple, skip windows, vol normalization, MA and extremes variants
Batch 3 cross the two improvements: skip recent window via delay or subtraction, and scale by slow volatility std(250), across horizons
Batch 4 tune skip length and vol denominator around the leading reversal signal, plus probe skew beta corrm families for diversifying alpha
Batch 5 refine leading reversal further and test structurally different families vol regime kurtosis drawdown extremes and short mom by long reversal interaction
Batch 6 map the vol amplified reversal surface and alternative reversal encodings via MA spreads and distance from rolling extremes

text: Approach so far. Batch 1 was a wide unbiased sweep of every raw feature family across the full lookback grid to find which effects exist and their signs. The dominant effect is intermediate to long horizon cross sectional reversal: ret(40) through ret(250) are all negatively predictive with a smooth monotone gradient, and the same effect shows up independently in ma(60..250), maxr(60..250) and minr(120..250), which is strong evidence it is a real panel property rather than a fitting artifact. Batches 2 to 6 refined it along three axes that each improved results consistently rather than at isolated points: (1) skipping the most recent 10 to 15 days via delay, which removes short horizon reversal and microstructure contamination and peaks smoothly at delay 10 to 15; (2) rescaling by trailing volatility, where both mul and div by std(250) improve on the raw signal, implying the gain is a cross sectional reweighting toward volatile names where reversal is stronger rather than a pure risk normalization; (3) blending adjacent horizons. I verified that cs_rank at the top level is a no op, confirming the harness scores only the cross sectional ordering. Secondary and largely independent effects: kurt(250) positive with a monotone gradient in lookback, skew(10) positive, corrm(250) weakly positive, std(250) weakly negative. Because many monotone reweightings of the same core signal all land in a 1.45 to 1.74 band, I treat differences inside that band as mostly noise and will select structurally central and economically motivated forms rather than the single train maximum, and will prefer signals whose whole neighbourhood scores well.

text: Final selection logic. The panel is dominated by one large effect, cross sectional reversal at intermediate horizons, which I confirmed from four independent encodings that were never fitted to each other: raw ret(40) to ret(250) all negative, ma(60) to ma(250) all positive, maxr(60) to maxr(250) negative, and minr(120) to minr(250) negative. Three structural refinements each improved results monotonically rather than at isolated grid points, which is the test I used to separate signal from fitting noise: skipping the last 10 days, scaling by a slow volatility or extremes measure, and blending the 40 and 60 day horizons. On top of that core I added three secondary effects that are each individually predictive standalone and therefore not spurious interactions: kurt(250) at SR 0.77 with a monotone gradient in lookback, skew at SR 0.47 to 0.73, and classic 5 day short term reversal at SR 0.34. The resulting six component equal weight rank composite scores 2.06 to 2.28 across every structural substitution I tried, including swapping the reversal denominator among maxr(250), maxr(120), std(250), std(60), std(20) and none at all, swapping simple for log returns, and moving the skew lookback across 10, 60, 120 and 250. That width is the main evidence for out of sample durability: the result is a plateau, not a spike, so no single arbitrary choice is load bearing. I deliberately did not report the three highest train scores, because they sit inside that plateau and their ordering is noise. Instead I report the top member of each of three different reversal encodings so the idiosyncratic component of any one scaling choice does not sink all three: the maxr(250) scaled version, a variant of it with a different short term reversal denominator, and the volatility multiplied version. I rejected additions that looked attractive on a single fit but lacked a supporting gradient, notably corrm and beta which degraded every composite despite positive standalone scores, and the low volatility tilt which also degraded the blend.

rationale: All three are equal weight cross sectional rank composites of the same six economically distinct blocks: intermediate horizon reversal at 40 and 60 days skipping the most recent 10 days, entered twice for horizon diversification, plus long run kurtosis, long run skew, 5 day short term reversal, and short run skew. The core reversal effect is corroborated by four independent encodings in the raw feature set: ret(40) through ret(250) all negatively predictive, ma(60) through ma(250) positively, and maxr and minr at 120 and 250 negatively, so it is a property of the panel rather than a fitted artifact. Each secondary block is independently predictive standalone at SR 0.34 to 0.77 with a monotone gradient in lookback, so the composite does not depend on any spurious interaction. Train SR for the three is 2.28, 2.20 and 2.16, but I did not select on rank within that band: every structural substitution I tested scored 2.06 to 2.28, so the composite sits on a wide plateau and the ordering inside it is noise. I therefore picked the top member of three different reversal encodings, maxr(250) scaled, a variant with a different short term reversal denominator, and volatility multiplied, so that no single arbitrary scaling choice is load bearing across all three. Additions with positive standalone scores but no supporting gradient, namely corrm, beta and the low volatility tilt, degraded the blend and were rejected.
